articles.title: From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and Tyapa
articles.summary: For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year journey from Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.
body: Tyapa (left) and Bu (right) were previously kept in small cages in the Republic of Dagestan in Russia

After years in cramped cages, two brown bears are adjusting to their new life following a remarkable rescue mission that spanned multiple countries, was disrupted by two major conflicts and involved more than 100 people.
For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year rescue journey from the Republic of Dagestan in Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.
One bear had spent their life forced to perform in a circus, while the other was confined to a cage so small they could not stand upright.
Today, the bears are now adjusting to a totally different world among the trees and grass at Wild Ireland, a sanctuary for rescued animals in County Donegal.
Tyapa is slowly settling into her new surroundings in Burnfoot, County Donegal
Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin first learned about Bu and Tyapa in 2021 and committed to bringing them to safety in Donegal.
The sanctuary, located in Burnfoot, opened in October 2019 and provides a safe space for animals, including brown bears, monkeys, wolves, and lynx.
Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin says the bears' health improvements since their arrival have been remarkable
McLaughlin said the two bears were in extremely poor health when they were first rescued.
Former circus bear Bu had spent years confined to a small indoor cage after being forced to perform.

McLaughlin said Tyapa had lived in a cage measuring just 2.5m by 2.5m by 2m, which was too low for him to stand upright and had no roof, which left him exposed to the harsh winters and blistering summer heat.
The bear had no water dish and relied on a hose for drinking water. McLaughlin said he was being raised to be killed for an eventual taxidermy display.
When the bears were rescued, both were severely malnourished and showed signs of psychological trauma.
Blood tests also revealed serious kidney problems associated with prolonged dehydration.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made the original transport route through Ukraine impossible, said McLaughlin.

An alternative route through the Middle East was then explored, but plans were disrupted again in February 2026 when the escalating conflict involving Iran led to airspace closures and flight disruptions across the region.

More than 100 people were involved in the rescue operation, including volunteers, lawyers, veterinarians, animal transport specialists, cargo teams and officials in Russia, the United Arab Emirates and Ireland.
The bears travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in the Republic of Ireland on 3 August 2026
In late October 2025, Dima and Yana Kim, who work at Tiger House, a sanctuary near St Petersburg that cares for former circus tigers, embarked on a 36-hour drive to Dagestan to rescue the bears.

Bu and Tyapa had to be cut out of their rusting steel cages, sedated and placed in secure transport crates for the journey back to Tiger House, where they received veterinary treatment and underwent quarantine.
After months of preparation and repeated delays, the bears eventually travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in Ireland in August.
Since arriving at Wild Ireland, McLaughlin said both bears have gained weight, their coats have improved, and follow-up blood tests have shown that their kidney function has returned to normal.
He said their habitat provides woodland, water and room to explore, as well as sheltered areas where they can retreat or move out of public view if they would like some privacy.
"These bears have suffered trauma and the first step of that recovery process is get them back out into the forest, get their paws into the soil and on the grass and get them exploring.
"We hope they can now have a full and happy life."
Working with bears is certainly not your everyday job, but for Wild Ireland team member Chloe McElhatton, it's one she absolutely relishes.
Chloe has been working at Wild Ireland for just over a year. She studied zoology at Queen's University Belfast, completing a four-year degree before joining the team.
"This is obviously a very unique job, and it's quite different from what most people would do," she said.
Chloe McElhatton is part of the bear team at Wild Ireland and says looking after bears is not your average 9-5 job

"We've done a lot of work hiding food around the bear habitats, encouraging them to search and forage for it themselves and this promotes their natural behaviours and helps them become more comfortable in that new open space," she said.
"Over time, we've seen their confidence build, and you can see great changes, both physically and mentally, in both of them."
Liam, who is from France, says the two bears are big and impressive
Liam, who is from France, said the bears were one of his favourite animals to see when visiting the park.
"Very big and very impressive," is how he summed up Bu and Tyapa.
"I saw chickens, some wolves and some monkeys and then the bears which were definitely my favourite."
Chris Roberts is a regular visitor to Wild Ireland and came to visit hoping to see a glimpse of the two new bears
Chris Roberts is from Manorcunningham, about 20 minutes from Wild Ireland, and has been visiting the site ever since it first opened in 2019.
"I've lost count of how many times we've been here, but we really wanted to come down today to see if we could catch a glimpse of Bu and Tyapa.
"It was fantastic to see them in the flesh.
"We absolutely loved it and are delighted to see them doing so well, especially considering their backstory and the awful conditions they were once kept in."

articles.title: Three released without charge after fatal arson attack in Ireland
articles.summary: Three people - two women and one man - have been released, and one person remains in custody, gardaí say.
body: Flowers have been left at the home where four people died after an arson attack in Waterford
Three people, who were arrested in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in the Republic of Ireland, have been released, gardaí (Irish police) have said.

Philip and Kim English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire earlier this month.
A man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s were previously charged in connection with the attack.
On Saturday, gardaí said three people - two women in their 30s and a man in his 50s - who were arrested on Tuesday have been released without charge.
A fourth person, a man in his 20s who was arrested on Thursday, remains in custody.

articles.title: Father who killed Oregon school gunman describes anguish over children he couldn't save
articles.summary: Kaylub Giamanco has been hailed as a hero for killing a teenager who fatally shot three children and a teacher.
body: Watch: Bystander who stopped Oregon school shooter describes how he approached gunman

A father who fatally shot a gunman at his daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described his anguish over being unable to save more pupils after "hearing children pleading for their lives".
Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by Kaylub Giamanco.

"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed, in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.
"The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."
Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".
He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life.
"I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.

The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.
Giamanco told OPB that the day of the attack began with breakfast and making packed lunches. He and his wife had spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.
The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.
He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.
Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services.
"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die'," he told the broadcaster.
He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building.
"I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.
Three schoolchildren and a teacher were killed in the shooting
Giamanco crawled through a shattered window and reached the classroom, where a teacher was locked in a struggle with the gunman. He opened the door and fired.
Giamanco told OPB he fired again when the attacker reached for his weapon. He then placed his own gun on the ground and raised his hands as an officer appeared.
He described feeling like the "last line of defence" between the children and the gunman, and said he "was supposed to be there" that day.
Afterwards, he called his wife to say he would not be home for lunch and that she needed to get to the school immediately. He then called his mother to tell her what had happened.
"Mum, I just had to take the life of what I think is might be a child because he ran into my daughter's school with a gun," he said.
Police identified the gunman as Griffin J John II - a former pupil who had attended special education classes at the school. His motive remains under investigation.

Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, aged five. His father said the family was "broken and lost".
Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job".
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.
The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request.
The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said in a statement shared with US media that the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door.

Teacher in Oregon shooting said she pretended to be dead to survive
Giamanco's name became public less than a day after the shooting. His mother, Kenda Freeman, read a family statement saying he was not seeking recognition and asking for privacy.
Shortly after the attack, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised his intervention while acknowledging its emotional cost.
"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she said.
Giamanco told OPB he now lies awake after his family goes to bed, replaying the attack.
"I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams."

articles.title: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
articles.summary: The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests to form the biggest challenge to Vučić's rule.
body: The Student List is Number 3 on Serbia's ballot paper, so the figure seen being hugged by this supporter has become a symbol of the movement's fight for change
If Sunday's parliamentary elections really are a battle for the heart of Serbia, then who better than a cardiologist to be one of the leading figures in the race.

Ilija Srdanović appears an unlikely opponent for Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić, arriving for an interview by motorbike sporting a fluorescent yellow jacket emblazoned with pro-student slogans.
He has been selected as top candidate for an opposition movement posing the most serious challenge to Vučić since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) entered government in 2012.

The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests led by young Serbians, outraged by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station's canopy collapsed in Serbia's second city Novi Sad.
What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election

Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list.
"It is absolutely normal to stand with my students to help them in their fair struggle," Srdanović told the BBC.
Ilija Srdanović tops the Student List's 250 candidates but would not necessarily lead Serbia if they won

The Student List is up against a Serbian leader who has served successively as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since 2012. When he called these snap elections last month, he stood down as president to run again for the role of prime minister.
Whatever Vučić's title, there has never been any doubt that he was the man in charge – an image enthusiastically promoted by Serbia's largely uncritical media.

He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.
Vučić has painted the student movement as foreign-backed and seeking to "bring down our state". "Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at a final campaign rally.

Just like the protest movement from which it developed, the Student List has no hierarchy or nominated leader. This makes it a proposition unlike any other in Serbia's relatively short democratic history.
Reliable polls are thin on the ground, but analysts are predicting an extremely tight vote.
A reported 150,000 supporters turned out for the final Student List rally in Belgrade's Slavija Square on Thursday night
Ilija Srdanović may head the list of candidates – but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won.

Srdanović insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time."

The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes – and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness.

"We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name.

"All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds.
The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage.

At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources".
The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response.
Vučić continues to command strong support among sections of Serbia's population

For the past 18 months, there has also been a full-time, pro-SNS camp in the small park between the National Assembly and the Presidency building in the centre of Belgrade. Its residents have repeatedly attacked journalists and made the park a no-go zone for local people.
Vučić has called the camp "a symbol of resistance" against those who "cannot stand different opinions".
But his major challenge remains what happened outside Novi Sad railway station two years ago.

The station's renovation was a key part of his signature infrastructure project – the high-speed line linking Belgrade and Budapest. So it has been difficult for Vučić to distance himself from the disaster.
Aleksandar Vučić stepped down as president last month with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister
Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands".
"This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED.
"Vučić has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy."
On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act.

Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China – both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.
Vučić has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power.
"When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally.
"You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart."

The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar Vučić as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates.
The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader – or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer.

articles.title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
articles.summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.
body: Canada and the US are currently locked in a tit-for-tat trade war

The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.
From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".
Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports.
The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".
It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".
Maine Senator Susan Collins is seeking to keep her seat in November's midterm elections
Trump "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce", White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said.

Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said: "While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."

The White House's announcement comes less than a fortnight before the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican Party or Democrats will control Congress, impacting the remaining two years of his term.

Collins said she had repeatedly asked senior Trump officials for tariff relief and that she would "continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner".
The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts
She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".

Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."

Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war.
Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.
Also on Friday, Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US.
Carney, who has sought closer ties with Europe since the tariff war erupted, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but was willing to wait it out.

"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC. "If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that."

LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

articles.title: Seven missing after multi-storey building collapses in Kenya's capital
articles.summary: Rescue efforts are under way to find people trapped under the block, which was still under construction when it buckled.
body: A search and rescue effort is under way to find seven people feared trapped under rubble after a building collapsed in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.
Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.

Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops that had opened at the base of the building.
The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.

The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.

Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.

Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.
Footage taken from nearby shows moments before (left) and moments after (right) the building collapsed

Rescue efforts have been complicated by concerns that excavation using diggers could limit the supply of air to those trapped, prompting emergency responders to cease using them, according to the Daily Nation newspaper.
Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations.

Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday.
Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied.
He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards".
Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.

articles.title: Trump administration sues to block certification of upcoming Alaska election
articles.summary: The justice department has filed a lawsuit arguing that the inclusion of two candidates named Dan Sullivan could confuse voters.
body: Senator Dan Sullivan, right, is in a tight race with Democratic contender Mary Peltola.

The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.
The justice department said in a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday that the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate.
Polls suggest the race between Senator Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is tight, with Peltola holding a narrow lead in the final days before the 3 November vote.
The US government wants the judge to bar the state from certifying the results if Senator Sullivan loses by a margin less than the other Sullivan.
"I'm the one that said do it," US President Donald Trump told reporters when asked for his thoughts on the lawsuit after he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday.

Trump has referred to the second Sullivan's candidacy as a "scam" and said his administration was looking at "powerful legal options" to end it. The retired teacher previously denied his candidacy had an ulterior motive.
Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.
For the 3 November midterm election, the senator will be listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent.
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.

In court documents, the justice department said Alaska "will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its elections" if it includes "any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan".
The second Sullivan, who was also a US Forest Service worker, was reportedly once a member of the Alaska Independence Party before registering as a Republican earlier this year.
In the filing, Associate Attorney General Stanley E Woodward Jr asserted that the sole purpose of his candidacy was to benefit Peltola's campaign by reducing the number of votes for the senator.

"Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Dan J Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity," Woodward argued.
Dan J Sullivan has repeatedly denied those claims, telling the local Petersburg Pilot newspaper earlier this year that he "wouldn't even know who to speak to" in Peltola's campaign.

He said separately to Courthouse News that it was his "sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but, ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running".

In the event Peltola wins, and the margin of loss suggests possible confusion, the lawsuit calls for certification to be delayed pending an investigation into whether voters were mixed up on the names as well as any "necessary and appropriate" steps to determine what would have happened had the second Sullivan been kept off the ballot.
Neither candidate has so far commented on the lawsuit.
The Senate race in Alaska - which Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024 - is among the most closely watched in the upcoming midterm elections.
The president's approval ratings in the state have been badly hit by voter disapproval of rising prices and the war in Iran.

articles.title: Minneapolis withdrawal was 'surrender', Trump's ex-border patrol chief tells BBC
articles.summary: Greg Bovino was the public face of the controversial immigration enforcement operation in the city earlier this year.
body: Watch: Trump's ex-border patrol chief challenged over Minneapolis operation

The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration.

In an interview with the BBC, Greg Bovino also said he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time".
Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.

The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city.

Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters.

One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence".

Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury, and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter".
A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless".
Watch: Renee Good's partner speaks publicly for first time since her death

Speaking in Detroit where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, Bovino said the administration "threw the towel in" and called for more deportations, which he said were now at a "virtual standstill".
He added that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota and arresting even more illegal aliens".
Bovino said his agents in Minneapolis were the "real victims" of what he called "the most violence that any law enforcement mission ever in the history of the United States has been up against".

Challenged by the BBC over how immigration agents handled both shooting incidents, Bovino rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined his claim that Good and Pretti had intended to harm the agents.
"The evidence is that violence was perpetrated against agents of the US government, and this is a society of laws and people need to follow the law. If not, there are consequences," he said.

Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake".
The withdrawal from Minnesota, which saw some 700 immigration agents leave the state, also saw Bovino removed from his post. The operation was taken over by the White House 'border tsar' Tom Homan.
When asked why he was removed, Bovino told the BBC: "You'd have to ask the administration. I still haven't gotten the final word on that."
Bovino recently addressed a rally by activists in Michigan who are calling for authorities to deport Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed
Kristi Noem, who was Homeland Security Secretary at the time of the operation, was fired by Trump in March.

Bovino has since retired from the US border patrol. He has become known for his hardline stance on immigration, often going further in his statements than Trump's own officials and claiming without evidence that 100 million people are illegally in the US and should be deported.

He has called for "total spectrum immigration enforcement" with support from the US military involving "cruise ships packed to the gills, cars, planes, trains, automobiles, all headed out of the United States packed with illegal aliens".
Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials
The ICE raids are over, but some Minnesotans say they still live in fear
Analysing the Minneapolis shooting frame by frame
Newly released video undermines ICE account of Minneapolis migrant shooting
When asked about Bovino's comments about Minneapolis, a White House spokesperson said "the president has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history".
"He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," they said.

Bovino has also floated "exploring" a presidential run in 2028. "If politicians aren't going to step up and do their job then you might see something happen," he told the BBC when asked about his intentions.

Bovino recently addressed a far-right rally by activists in Michigan who are calling for authorities to deport Abdul El-Sayed, a US citizen and Democratic candidate running in the state's tightly fought race for a Senate seat.
American-born Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the Senate if he wins the seat against Republican Mike Rogers.

articles.title: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
articles.summary: Ukraine and Russia confirm the truce in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where residents have had to eat garden weeds to survive.
body: These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year
US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.
The statement said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" would begin on 29 October.

"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," it added. Ukraine and Russia later confirmed the ceasefire was agreed.

Oleshky, in the Kherson region, was seized by Russian forces during the first days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Remaining residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.
Trump: First lady's 'initiative' led to truce for Ukraine city
The White House statement said Melania Trump and her representative had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".
The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.

Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky's party in parliament, later said "an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surroundings will begin in the near future".
"To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," he said.
In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman confirmed the truce had been agreed.
"The military is currently working to coordinate the timings of a ceasefire," Dmitry Peskov said. "Those who wish to do so will be able to leave this settlement."
Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions
Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.
They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.
Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.

The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.
The city was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.

While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".
Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children.

In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa.
Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July.
According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace.
"I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year.
"And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home'."

articles.title: Six shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say
articles.summary: Another 28 people are injured in the southern Karak governorate, and a manhunt is now under way.
body: Between 150 and 200 people were in the church at the time of the shooting, one witness told the AFP news agency
Six people were killed when gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, a government spokesperson has said.
Another 28 people were injured in the church in the village of Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.

The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing, in what government spokesperson Dr al-Momani Mohammad described as a "heinous attack".
Jordan's King Abdullah II said the authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties."
Dozens of people had been inside the church for the funeral when the shooting began, Khaled Burqan, one of the mourners, told Jordan's al-Mamlaka state-run TV.
He said two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol had been firing at the mourners for several minutes.
CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.

Two of the attackers are seen making their way onto what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.
Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid some chaotic scenes.
No-one has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.
Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near church
A news briefing by interior ministry officials is expected shortly, and al-Momani has said the country's prime minister will chair a meeting of the Security Council to be attended by all ministers.

In his post on X, King Abdullah II offered his condolences to the families of the victims, writing: "Whoever imagines that the bullets of treachery can divide the ranks of Jordanians will fail in his endeavour before our steadfastness and unity."

Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media.
Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.
Such violence is rare in Jordan, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the country in the past.

articles.title: Argentina drops investigation into President Milei over crypto fraud
articles.summary: Javier Milei had denied acting fraudulently when a cryptocurrency nosedived after he deleted a social media post about it.
body: Javier Milei had denied crypto fraud allegations
A criminal investigation into Argentine President Javier Milei and his sister's links to a cryptocurrency scandal has been dropped.
The case against Milei and his sister Karina Milei was dismissed by federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi at the request of prosecutors, court records show.
The Argentinian president had denied promoting the newly launched cryptocoin $Libra , which collapsed shortly after he mentioned it in a social media post in February 2025.

He said he had acted "in good faith" when the cryptocurrency rose in value before crashing and causing huge losses for the majority of its investors. Milei is yet to respond to news of the case being dropped.
Dismissing the case, the judge said "the reported events do not fall under a legal category", and concluded that no "criminally relevant deception" had been proven.
Accusations of fraud arose when Milei posted on X, formerly Twitter, about the $Libra coin, which he said at the time would help fund small businesses and start-ups.
The cryptocurrency's price subsequently shot up when the Argentine president shared a link to buy it.
But, within a few hours, he deleted his post and the crypto nosedived in value, losing investors most of their money.

It led opposition members of Congress to plan impeachment proceedings, while some online accused Milei of a "rug pull" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales.
The Argentinian president, though, insisted: "I didn't promote it, I merely shared it" in an interview with local media Todo Noticias'.
The presidential office insisted that Milei was in no way involved in the development of $Libra and announced that the Anti-Corruption Office would determine if the president had acted improperly.
Milei himself defended deleting his post, saying that at the time he did not know "the details of the project and after learning about it, I decided not to continue promoting it".
And, in a TV interview, he insisted that those who invested in $Libra had done so "voluntarily" and knew of the risks.

articles.title: At least one dead and four injured in Paris suburb shooting
articles.summary: The French prime minister says an individual is in police custody after a "serious event" in Trappes.
body: One person has been killed and four others injured in a Parisian suburb, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said.
The "very serious events" happened in Trappes, to the west of Paris, Lecornu wrote on social media, adding that the suspected attack had been "apprehended and placed in police custody".
A police source said a man opened fire from a vehicle on Friday, according to news agency AFP, and was later arrested in the nearby town of Coignières at about 10:30 local time (08:30 GMT).
Reports in French media suggest the number of injured may be higher and that a 12-year-old child may be among them.
Lecornu said the National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office has announced it is monitoring the situation.

articles.title: Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
articles.summary: Ukrainians held alongside the American say they witnessed beatings and sexual humiliation by Russian guards during his detention.
body: Stephen Hubbard (second from left in the first row) was flown back home on a US plane earlier this week
Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.
Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.
"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."
Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.
"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."
Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.

He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.
Ihor Shyshko alleges that Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of Russian prison staff
Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.
"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.
"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."
Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.
Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.
The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.
Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.
Dmytro Khyliuk says Hubbard was hidden in a Russian prison to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors
Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.
He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.
Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.
"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.
Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.
"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.

"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."
They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.
"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.
Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.
"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."
Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.
He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.

"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".
Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.
"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.
But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".
Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.
"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".
Hubbard was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024, accused of serving in a defence unit in eastern Ukraine

articles.title: Oil spill washes up on UAE beaches after tanker strike
articles.summary: Satellite images show oil spreading for miles along the coastline, threatening local marine wildlife
body: An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.

Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran.
The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.
UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.
The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".

Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.
Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.
But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.
Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.
They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.

Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.

But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.
The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.
BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.

Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.
Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.
Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.
The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.
All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.
Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October.

Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.
Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.
Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August, which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.

articles.title: Brazilians vote in presidential election runoff pitting leftist Lula against far-right Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Incumbent president lost in first round to senator and son of convicted ex-president
body: Brazilians are going to the polls on Sunday in a highly unpredictable runoff in which the leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is attempting an unprecedented comeback against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who won the first-round vote.
Bolsonaro’s surprise victory despite not leading most polls made him the favourite three weeks ago, but since then Lula’s campaign has gained ground, and the two go into the contest virtually tied.

The gap between them was the narrowest ever recorded in a first round, at less than 2% of the vote, and the 81-year-old president has spent much of the runoff campaign focused on turnout – abstention reached a record high in the first round and disproportionately affects his voters – and on stoking fears over what a return to power by a member of the Bolsonaro family could mean.
Related: Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensifies days before Brazil presidential runoff

A congressman for more than 20 years with few bills passed, the 45-year-old Bolsonaro is the eldest son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup to overturn his 2022 defeat to Lula.

The senator has promised that if elected he will pardon his father, and with an even more conservative congress taking office next year he has vowed to “change the constitution and re-democratise this country”, sending chills through those who fear he could follow in his father’s authoritarian footsteps.

“We’re facing two completely different projects for the country,” said voter Nuno Rau, 63, an architect and writer. “One points towards the end of social rights and the end of democracy itself; on the other side is someone who fought for income distribution and free public education. I may have criticisms of Lula, but there is no way to choose Bolsonaro,” he added.

Aparecida Moreira, a 62-year-old lawyer, will vote for Bolsonaro mainly because of the “iron fist” security policy he proposes, including building five “mega-prisons” inspired by those of El Salvador’s populist autocrat Nayib Bukele.

“I agree with Bolsonaro’s idea of chemical castration for rapists, because there is no crime worse than rape,” said Moreira, adding that voting for Lula would be the same as voting for the “dictator” Alexandre de Moraes, the justice who, despite not having been appointed by Lula, is widely associated with him by Bolsonaro supporters because he oversaw the former president’s conviction.
Both Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula drew large crowds to their final campaign rallies on Saturday in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo and Belo Horizonte.
With each side of supporters virtually “crystallised”, the election will be decided by the small number of voters who identify with neither candidate.
Bolsonaro began the runoff campaign with a lead and the support of most other defeated candidates, but instead of growing, he stagnated in the polls while Lula gained support.

Many analysts saw this as the result of part of the population suddenly waking up to the “fear” of a Bolsonaro returning to power, as well as controversies including the fact that the senator is under investigation in two federal police inquiries over alleged corruption and money laundering.
Lula, by contrast, radically changed his digital strategy and benefited from student-led protests across the country, most of which did not even involve the president.

“In the first round, Lula’s campaign failed to connect with the population, but now it has been civil society movements that have driven his growth,” said the political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.
Whatever the result, the race is expected to be decided by a narrow margin in Latin America’s largest country, with an electorate of 159 million.

Many analysts believe that if Lula overturns his first-round defeat, Bolsonaro could follow his father’s example from four years ago and refuse to concede, and that Donald Trump, a longstanding ally of the Bolsonaro clan, could refuse to recognise the result.

“Trump wants to ‘colonise’ all of Latin America in pursuit of its own interests,” said Telles, adding that, with rightwing candidates having won all seven presidential elections held in Latin America since Trump began his second term, Brazil is one of the few countries in the region still offering any resistance to the US president.
“So a Bolsonaro victory would mean losing Brazil to a model of autocracy backed by the US,” she added.

articles.title: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes
articles.summary: PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint
body: Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.

The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.

Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.
People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.

The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20-minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.

Israeli elections will take place in four days and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.
Related: Heidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attack

Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.
Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.

A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.

A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”
Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.

“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”

The Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) said in a written statement that approximately 2,000 residents of the target area belonged to a clan which the IDF said was “associated with Hamas and from which the terrorists who carried out yesterday’s attack originated”.
“As part of the operation, civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area through designated screening points staffed by the ISA and IDF soldiers,” the statement said.

Separately, the IDF said, it was carrying out demolitions near the site of Friday’s attack, saying it was tearing down “infrastructure and structures built in violation of the law, in order to enforce law and order and remove potential security risks posed by these structures”.

articles.title: ‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder’: Palestinians fear the worst from Israel election
articles.summary: Humanitarian catastrophe largely ignored as rivals Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu vow to end Hamas rule
body: As Israel prepares to go to the polls, Palestinians in Gaza are bracing for an outcome that could shape their future, knowing their fate rests with the country that has reduced much of the territory to rubble and killed nearly 75,000 people.
Gaza, where nearly a million displaced Palestinians face dire sanitary conditions, water shortages and the constant threat of Israeli strikes, has been largely absent from the election campaign.

Both Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition Yashar party have focused instead on the goal of destroying Hamas in the wake of the 7 October attacks and the trauma inflicted on Israeli society. The humanitarian catastrophe unfolding just across the border has received little, if any, attention.

“We hope a government will come to power that is less inclined towards killing, displacement and our extermination,” said Sami Abu Rumi, 47, from Rafah, who is now displaced in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. “But, ultimately, we see the thinking of Israeli governments as largely similar.”
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has set out a clear plan for Gaza’s future. Both have vowed to end Hamas rule and both support Donald Trump’s controversial peace plan.
Eisenkot, the former military chief whose party is leading Netanyahu’s Likud in the polls, has pledged to restore Israel’s international standing after three years of war. Yet he is no dove.

A senior commander during Israel’s 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot, whose son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza, later championed the “Dahiya doctrine”, which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated. Critics say the strategy has since been employed in Gaza, causing widespread destruction that, they argue, amounts to war crimes.

“Eisenkot talks of defeating Hamas, while Netanyahu boasts about military operations and the killing of Palestinians,” said Abu Rumi. ‘‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder. Meanwhile, families here struggle to feed their children, keep them in school and access medical care. With homes and infrastructure destroyed, simply surviving has become a daily struggle.”

Earlier this week, the Arab-led Joint List party in Israel aired a 48-second election video showing drone footage of Gaza’s ruins. “[We] behave as if everything that has happened here is completely normal,” the voiceover says. “As if tens of thousands of people weren’t killed here … as if entire cities were not destroyed and turned into wastelands.”
The party vows it “will not be silent”, adding: “[The other parties] want more destruction. We offer life.”
Related: ‘The biggest motivation is fear’: High turnout among Israel’s Palestinians could unseat Netanyahu

The chances of Arab parties joining an Eisenkot-led coalition are slim to none, although they could offer support from outside government. Yet among Palestinians in Gaza, pessimism runs deep: whoever wins, little is expected to change.

“I do not believe anyone genuinely cares about Gaza or has its people’s interests at heart,’’ said Haneen Hamdouna, 45, from Beit Lahia, who has also been displaced to al-Mawasi. ‘‘Whether it is Netanyahu, Eisenkot or someone else, attacking Gaza seems to have become part of Israeli election campaigning.

“For years, we have said that the incoming government might be better than the one before it, only to be shocked when it turns out to be worse. Perhaps 200 trucks would be allowed into Gaza instead of 100, but that would not mean any real change in our lives.”

In Gaza, most people are too preoccupied by the struggle to find food and water to follow the election campaign. Fears of renewed hunger are mounting as markets run short of fresh produce and other essentials.

Residents say commercial deliveries have been suspended for about a week, driving up prices. Flour now costs more than three times its previous price, while dwindling humanitarian aid has left families increasingly vulnerable to another food crisis.
Yet, some people in Gaza are following the Israeli elections closely, driven less by hope of change than fear of what the outcome could mean for their future.

They fear that Palestinian suffering has become a recurring feature of Israeli election campaigns, with candidates competing over who can take the toughest stance towards Gaza rather than offering any prospect of a better future.

“A friend was supposed to hold his son’s wedding in the coming days,” said Karim Mareesh, 43. “But he decided to postpone it until after the Israeli elections. He feared that the far-right government might secure another term, prompting the war to resume and forcing him to flee again. He could lose his tent and the wedding supplies he had struggled to save up for.”

Hope is hard to find in Gaza, where three years of war have reduced entire neighbourhoods to wastelands of shattered concrete and bomb craters. It is harder still to imagine a future when Israeli restrictions on food and humanitarian aid have turned hunger into a weapon of war. And almost impossible to see any light at the end of the tunnel when more than 20,000 Palestinian children have been killed since 7 October 2023.

“I feel that everything said about addressing our suffering is nothing more than an attempt to soothe our pain, or simply words and promises that we no longer believe,” says Noor AlMoghanni, 20, from Gaza City.
“Whether Netanyahu wins or loses, the reality here will not change. As I see it, their goal is to destroy Gaza and the foundations of life here.”

articles.title: Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says
articles.summary: Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders
body: Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.

“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”

After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”

Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.

The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.

Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.

Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.

“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”

Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.

Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.
Related: Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar | Steve Bloomfield

Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.
He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.

“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”
The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.

Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.

“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

articles.title: Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions
articles.summary: But Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX owns Starlink, accuses Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms
body: Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.

But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for ⁠offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a social media post.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, said on the Telegram app that the country is “physically unable” to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations.
Ukraine’s general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment.

The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.

The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.

The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.

However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”

Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.

The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”
There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.
Related: Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming whom in the Ukraine-Starlink row?

Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for ‌today is that Starlink ‌and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the ‌level we need.”

The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
