On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.

When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”
He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.

articles.title: More than one million Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff
articles.summary: Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro
body: More than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro.
Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%.

On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.

Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president, who was first elected in 2002, would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”
“The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.

“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.
“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.

Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, was president from 2019 to 2022, as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.

However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.

Some experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally – which Rio’s City Hall said attracted about 1.1 million people – activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”
On Saturday afternoon, Lula attended an even larger rally on Paulista Avenue, in the heart of Brazil’s biggest city, São Paulo.
“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo in Rio.

Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s father botched the response to Covid during his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.
“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.

Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.
Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.
Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.
Related: Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril | George Monbiot

“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.
Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.
“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.

“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.

Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”
“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.

Large crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.

Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.
“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.

“I don’t want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward,” Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US after Donald Trump’s January invasion, he said: “True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn’t been installed yet. It’s in transition.”
Antonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: “Lula did nothing for the country.”

Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws – which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs – whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. “Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same,” said Costa Jr.
Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio’s paramilitary “militia” groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.
“If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship,” said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: “Don’t let the mobsters win.”

articles.title: We want you! ADF recruitment rates are growing, even as the odds of conflict rise. Why are people signing up?
articles.summary: The number of full-time personnel across navy, army and air force grew to more than 64,000 this year, making it the largest military in 25 years
body: We’re herded into a sterile elevator by a woman in navy camouflage fatigues and carried up to the 11th floor, overlooking Parramatta’s central business district on a dreary afternoon in Sydney’s west.
At the front of the room, dressed in a khaki green uniform behind a lectern, stands army corporal Joel Kellner. In the corner, a portrait of King Charles III rests on a wooden easel.

“We’ll start with a rabble rouser,” Kellner says in a raspy drawl, clicking the projector into gear. A fighter jet roars over the ocean. Keyboards rattle in a neon-lit situation room. Soldiers blast their way through a doorway with explosives. Cue pulsing soundtrack and energetic voiceover:
Do more than send emails. Send critical intelligence.
When you travel for work. Travel undetected.
And if you work late. Work to defend what matters.
You get paid to finish the degree. No study debt. It puts you in a good position

The slick advertisement is a pitch to the room, an audience of mostly young men, a handful of young women, and their parents and carers – a crowd reflecting the ethnic diversity of western Sydney. It’s a small turnout of about 30 people. But this Australian defence force recruitment session, open to all and one of hundreds held across the country each month, forms the frontline of a much larger effort.

Facing what the government describes as the “most complex and threatening strategic circumstances” since the end of the second world war, Australia is investing billions to strengthen its maritime firepower in response to an increasingly contested Indo-Pacific region. The build-up includes long-range missile systems, army landing craft and the nuclear-powered submarines planned under the Aukus pact. To operate and maintain this equipment, the military now needs thousands more people. Will any of the young people in this room answer the call of duty?

“Serving your country, it gives you a sense of importance,” says Angad Sahi. The 16-year-old’s family migrated from northern India to Australia three decades ago and now live in Penrith in western Sydney. He’s in year 12 studying business, finance, law and advanced maths and, at 6ft 1 tall, is a keen basketball player.

He listens as Kellner outlines the more than 300 jobs on offer across the navy, army and air force. “My parents saw a lot of ads on social media about it … they looked into it and saw the benefits,” Sahi says.

With more than 8,100 new recruits , the number of full-time personnel across navy, army and air force grew to more than 64,000 this year. It’s the largest military in 25 years, though still a fraction of the scale of the mass mobilisations during world wars. The growth reverses years of recruitment and retention failures but still falls short of the government’s annual recruitment targets. Even so, Defence says it’s on track to grow to 69,000 full-time personnel by the early 2030s.
Related: Paul Keating says Aukus locking Australia into a US war against China, which it would ‘certainly lose’

A 2025 study by University of Tasmania’s Prof Robert Hoffman, commissioned by the ADF to examine declining sign-ups, concluded that a range of measures – including targeted advertising aimed at 16 to 25-year-olds on TikTok and video games, improved pay and conditions, and tweaking eligibility criteria, all seem to be contributing to the recruitment uptick. The surge in sign-ups is mirrored across the US, Germany and the United Kingdom (where there was a 19% rise in people joining the armed forces last year). And Canada’s defence forces have seen a 10-year high in recruitment, up by 55%.

And while Sahi does seem attracted to the concept of duty, it’s ultimately pragmatic reasons that makes the proposition appealing. “You get paid to finish the degree. No study debt. It puts you in a good position in the future, even once you leave.”

Sahi is talking about the Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA), where cadets earn a salary while completing a university degree and officer training, in exchange for a commitment to serve in the military for a minimum of about nine years after graduating. In the first year of study the pay is about $55,000. Once you graduate, you can easily earn more than $100,000 as a commissioned officer.

For the more non-committal types, the army gap year program offers a 12-month trial of military life. It appeals to year 12 student Eli Holt, 17, from the Sutherland shire. His favourite subject is sports science and, outside of school, he takes martial arts classes. “I like the idea of the discipline, the fitness, the money,” Holt says. “I’d be getting a taste for it and really seeing if I want to turn it into a career.
“And the army feels irreplaceable. Like there’s things that need to be done that AI just can’t do. That’s a comforting idea.”

Prof Ben Edwards of the ANU’s Centre for Social Policy Research says: “As the labour market gets tighter … [more young people] might see the ADF as an attractive option post-school.” Cost-of-living pressures and housing unaffordability may also influence their decisions.

But even signing up on the spot won’t fast-track a quick pathway to enlistment for any of the young people here this afternoon. In October 2026, the average time from lodging an application to enlistment was 259 days.

Jennifer Parker, adjunct professor at UWA’s Security Institute and former navy officer, says a cumbersome recruitment process involving exams, security screenings, medical examinations and interviews is a major bottleneck to the ADF’s growth.
“People coming out of school or university don’t want to wait around for a year to know if they can join or not,” Parker says.
The head of military personnel, Rear Admiral Letitia Van Stralen, told the Guardian that “significant reforms” are under way to reduce the application-to-enlistment period to 100 days on average.

As part of their current recruitment drive, Defence has also widened the pool of potential recruits. In 2024, it changed the standards so medical conditions such as acne or a childhood broken bone that had previously disqualified applicants could be assessed on a case-by-case basis, and eligibility has since been expanded to permanent residents from New Zealand, the UK, the US, Canada. And, from next month, Australia will open recruitment to Papua New Guinea university students as part of a new military alliance between the two countries. The first cohort of the $65m pilot program will be enlisted by next year.

The ADF have undergone significant attempts at reputation rehabilitation over the last few years amid scrutiny over its culture, including the Brereton inquiry into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan and the royal commission into defence and veteran suicide. And last week the ADF launched its first women veterans’ strategy, aimed at improving recognition, safety and economic security for women during and after service, and has adopted a target of 25% female workforce participation by 2030. Currently just over 20% of the workforce is female.

When Parker joined the navy back in 2002, women had only been at sea for 10 years. “Now the fleet commander is a woman. That just goes to show how much the ADF has evolved in its treatment of women,” she says.
We’d rather he have proper training than be suddenly conscripted

Female participation in the navy, like the air force, is much higher than the army, which lags at 15% participation. “I had a very positive career,” Parker says. “As a country we have struggled with equality for women, and the harassment of women. The ADF is drawn from wider society and therefore reflects that. That’s not in any way to excuse bad behaviour but it’s important to understand.”

Efforts have been made to stem the flow of departures from the military too. The military separation rate has fallen to its lowest level in 15 years, which Defence attributes to retention bonuses, improved housing and better working conditions.

Parker says these benefits, combined with one of the most significant modernisations in military history, make it a “fairly exciting time” to join the military. But, she warns, “anyone who joins the ADF should expect to serve on operations and, if necessary, be called upon to fight for their country – the chances of doing that is increasing”.
Eli Holt’s mother, Tara, and father, James, are seated beside him for the information session. They have some reservations. “We’re learning with him,” Tara says.
James says: “At first we weren’t a fan of the idea but we know we’re going to have to support him either way.

“The way we came to grips with it was, if there is a conflict, it’s probably going to be major and they’ll probably end up conscripting anyway … We’d rather he have proper training than be suddenly conscripted.”

Parental attitudes are the strongest predictor of a young person’s interest in serving. According to a Defence-funded report co-authored by Edwards, if a young person thinks their parents want them to enlist they are 30 times more likely to want to join themselves.

Parker says it’s unhelpful to speculate about exactly how Australia might enter a conflict. But Albert Palazzo, a military historian and adjunct professor at UNSW Canberra is more explicit. He says a potential US-China war over Taiwan is the most likely scenario to draw Australia into conflict. Because the US has access to or controls most of Australia’s military bases, Palazzo argues Australia would have little choice but to join the war.
Related: Grassroots Labor group urges Albanese government to chart course away from ‘American war machine’

“Australia has a long history of inviting itself to American wars. We’re now inviting ourselves to war with China,” Palazzo says. “It would be really ugly, violent. A lot of our people will die, young people. That’s the nature of war.”
At the recruitment session in Parramatta, the prospect of conflict feels distant. Glossy recruitment ads promise free health and dental care, subsidised housing and lifelong friends.

When the presentation ends, Kellner informs the group that they can apply online and offers an opportunity to come up the front and ask questions before leaving. The military’s policy of “unrestricted service”, which legally obliges personnel to be available at all times to deploy in Australia or overseas, is not discussed. That will come later in the recruitment process.
Mahmood Dakkak, 18, is in his first year of a university degree, studying to be high school history teacher, but is now considering a career in the navy.
“I kind of feel unfulfilled in life. I was looking online and saw jobs to work on nuclear submarines. Sounds pretty interesting,” Dakkak says.
But, worried about the increasing likelihood of war, he says he wants to avoid enlisting in a frontline role.

Holt admits it’s a consideration for him, too. “My dad believes that world war three might be sooner than later, even if I get out [after the gap year] I’d be on the roll [for 10 years] and drafted before any of my mates, that’s scary to think about,” he says.

The last person to file out of the room is 21-year-old Keriyacous Magar, who works in waste management in Sydney’s south-west. He’s attracted to the military by a good salary and the idea of a fulfilling career but admits: “I’m a bit confused.
“I’m just a young man trying to figure out where he wants to go in the world.”

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing
articles.summary: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres
body: Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.

The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.

But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.
Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them.
Related: Major protests in Paris and other French cities in challenge to Macron – in pictures

Police fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and another in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off.
The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests.

Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called “high-risk groups” who “broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence”.

More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.
At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”

A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”

The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said.

The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry.

At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue.
Related: NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France game

Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”

Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them, and we have to stand together.”

She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”

In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.

articles.title: Suspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in Bavaria
articles.summary: About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern Germany
body: Police have arrested a 33-year-old German citizen after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed.

About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany.
Flames rose high into the air as firefighters approached the scene to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said, adding that nobody was injured in the fire.
Lisa Maier, a police spokesperson, said firefighters struggled to tackle the blaze due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft).
The building, which was one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.
Built by the Nazis and formally inaugurated by Hitler on his birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest has been preserved as a monument to “the insanity of the regime”, according to its website.

The building is only accessible via a road cut into the mountain through previously impassable terrain. Nazis would enter a tunnel and take a 124-metre brass lift buried in the mountain to get inside the building.

Authorities were alerted to the fire when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.15pm, police said. When firefighters arrived on the scene at about 9.50pm, the entire building was engulfed in flames.
Fire departments from six municipalities sent emergency personnel to tackle the blaze and the Bavarian Red Cross, the local mountain rescue service and the police also attended.
No reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that investigators suspected it was the result of arson. Firefighters found no one inside the building.
Efforts to fight the fire were hampered by a strong wind and rain, which turned into the year’s first snow, and firefighters had to pull out overnight after several hours.
The blaze was reportedly still burning at 7am on Saturday but appeared to be out later in the morning, although smoke continued to rise from the building.

A police spokesperson told the German tabloid Bild: “It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved.” Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an Agence France-Presse photographer.
Maier said police were still investigating and would hold a news conference later on Saturday.

The 33-year-old suspect arrested by the police was a German citizen who had ties to the area but did not live there. Prosecutors said he showed signs of mental illness and after being questioned he was being sent to a psychiatric facility.
The possibility of a political motive for the blaze would be investigated, but police said there was nothing to indicate anyone else was involved.

The Eagle’s Nest was constructed between 1937 and 1938 and forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in the Holocaust.
It became legendary in the postwar period and was often depicted as an essential meeting place in US war films, although in reality Hitler rarely visited the complex.
Since 1952 the building has housed an exhibition by the Institute for Contemporary History recounting its Nazi history, and a restaurant.
Officials indicated that the building, which is owned by Bavaria’s state government, would be restored after discussions with local officials, historians and conservators.
“We’re not going to leave a ruin there,” Joachim Herrmann, Bavaria’s interior minister, told reporters, adding that it was important to continue to do “the work of remembrance”.
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title: Kim Jong-un crosses newly opened bridge into China
articles.summary: North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member
body: Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour.

The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency.
He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship.

Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua.
Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said.
Related: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?

The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950.

Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.
Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.

The 3km bridge opened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border, leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.

The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.

Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.
Xi will host the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.
Reuters reported on Friday, however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.
Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: Storm Boelo to bring 80mph gusts and heavy rain to parts of UK
articles.summary: Second named storm will hit northern parts of UK as thousands remain without power after Friday’s Storm Austen
body: The UK is bracing for a second storm this weekend, as strong winds and heavy rain are expected to disrupt travel and cause further power cuts in the north.
Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, is expected to bring heavy, frequent showers and winds potentially exceeding 80mph to northern parts of the UK.
Thousands of homes in the south-west of England have already been left without power after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday.
The Met Office has advised people to stay indoors as much as possible and said the storm will bring danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.

The forecaster has issued an amber alert, its second most severe weather warning, covering Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm Saturday to the same time on Sunday. Another amber warning is also in place for the north-east of Northern Ireland from 9pm Saturday to 10am Sunday.
Related: How autumnal high pressure brings on the dark doldrums

A large yellow warning for very wet and windy weather will cover the whole of the UK’s north from midday Saturday to 9pm on Sunday. Another warning for heavy rain covers Wales and parts of western and southern England from 11am to 11pm Saturday.

Widespread travel disruption is expected on ferries and trains. TransPennine Express has warned against making all but essential train journeys on Saturday and Sunday, while Avanti West Coast has strongly advised users not to travel north of Preston on Sunday.
The Met Office has also warned that power cuts across the south-west of England could be replicated across amber areas in the north this weekend.
In the south-west of England, 31,000 homes were without power at one stage on Friday. More than 3,700 were still without electricity on Saturday morning, according to the National Grid map.

Human-driven climate change has continued to reshape rainfall patterns and weather conditions globally. The UK experienced its hottest summer on record this year, with five heatwaves and a record-breaking 40 days of temperatures above 30C.

The Met Office meteorologist Alex Burkill said: “Storm Boelo is arriving. It’s going to bring widespread rain and some very strong winds indeed, and it’s quick on the tails of Storm Austen which is now clearing away towards the east.

“It’s the winds that were perhaps most concerned about, they’re really going to whip up some strong gusty winds across Northern Ireland, northern parts of England and also Scotland through the day – strengthening as we head towards the evening.

“Temperatures will be a little more than the seasonal average but obviously with the wind and rain it’s going to feel pretty unpleasant out there,” Burkhill added. “A very, well, different side of autumn compared with what we’ve seen through much of the season so far.”
Storm Boelo’s winds are expected to peak from Saturday evening. The wet weather will clear overnight in many areas, while more rain continues to hit Scotland and northern Ireland.
Attending a summit on the summer’s record wildfires on Friday, Andy Burnham warned that the UK could face “a winter of greater flooding”.

The prime minister denied suggestions that the government was playing catch-up with civil preparedness, but said “we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common”.

articles.title: ‘Bolso shows all signs of fascism’: the journalist who predicted Brazil’s future – and paid the ultimate price
articles.summary: Dom Phillips warned that Jair Bolsonaro would make life more dangerous for reporters and the Amazon rainforest, and that his sons were even more extreme
body: “Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters,” the murdered British journalist Dom Phillips told me before his death. “His sons are all more extreme if anything.”

These words were written in 2018 by the Guardian contributor shortly before the election of the far-right former army captain Jair Bolsonaro as president of Brazil – a prospect that Dom viewed with dread.

As he predicted back then, this would lead to more mortalities, more destruction of the Amazon rainforest and more danger for journalists. His own life and death were to prove the prescience of this foresight.

Dom was killed four years ago alongside the Brazilian indigenous expert Bruno Pereira, but his views feel alarmingly relevant once more as Brazil braces for a presidential runoff this Sunday in which a member of the far-right Bolsonaro clan is once more a favourite to win – despite all the dangers that poses to the environment and those who seek to protect it.
Related: One year after the deaths of Bruno Pereira and Dom Phillips, their work must go on

Polls suggest Flávio Bolsonaro – the son of Jair Bolsonaro – is narrowly ahead of the Workers party incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Although the difference between them is within the margin of error and Lula appears to have gained momentum, the possibility of another Bolsonaro administration is likely to fill any friends of Dom and Bruno with alarm.

Dom was no diehard political leftist. In an earlier election, he shocked me by expressing support for the centre-right challenger Aécio Neves because he felt the then Workers party administration had become too entangled in corruption. But while Dom eschewed ideology, he had clear ideas about the importance of sound, considerate government in the interests of people and the planet.
He saw the Bolsonaro family as a menace to both. Looking back through our exchanges of WhatsApp messages, I am struck by the prescience of his observations.

Some may be inclined to normalise Flávio as just another candidate, or to assume that all politicians are as bad as each other. That was certainly not how Dom saw things – and he came to pay the ultimate price for his efforts to address those concerns.

“I don’t think I have ever been so negative about Brazil’s future. Spent a week in Manaus, everyone seemed to be voting for Bolsonaro,” he wrote ahead of the first-round vote in 2018. “ If he wins, what would it be like living here? It’s like a ‘carte blanche’ to attack anyone his mob disagrees with.”
Related: ‘This is a lethal threat’: Indigenous groups fear Bolsonaro’s hold on voters in Brazil’s Amazon towns

Two weeks later, he observed the creeping hostility towards the media at a Bolsonaro press conference, which he said was packed with rightwing supporters who loudly booed a journalist that they considered unfriendly.
This followed a physical attack on the organiser of an anti-Bolsonaro women’s group. “Chilling times here,” he wrote on 12 October of that year.
“I agree that Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters.
“This is a very dark and worrying period and it is only going to get worse. My sense if [sic] that it is also going to become more dangerous for journalists.”

He detailed the changes he was already seeing – the proliferation of lies, a hardening of discourse online and a rising sense that violence was acceptable. He predicted more people would die as a result of Bolsonaro’s policies, and the wider environment would also pay a heavy price.

Over the following years, Dom’s reports for the Guardian confirmed his worst fears. Bolsonaro’s mismanaged response to the Covid crisis contributed to more than 704,000 deaths – the second highest toll in the world after the US.

His four years in power saw the highest level of Amazon deforestation of any presidential terms. Orwellian misinformation campaignsincluded efforts to blame environmental groups for forest fires and to boast – contrary to all the evidence – that his government was saving the Amazon.

In August 2019, Dom told me these claims were “staggering even by Bolsonaro standards, especially given Flávio Bolsonaro’s bill to get rid of legal reserves”, the latter a reference to a proposal by the then president’s son – and now presidential candidate – to remove one of the greatest protections for the rainforest.

Dom also came under social media attack after he politely asked the president about Amazon deforestation at a press conference. Bolsonaro snapped back, “the Amazon is Brazil’s, not yours, OK?” – a reply that was instantly spread across networks to suggest the nationalist had bested the foreigner.
Dom felt he had been set up. “The smile doesn’t last for long,” he observed. “Wonder how much of the Amazon will be gone by the end of Bolsonaro’s first term?”
Related: Brazil’s election and the battle for the Amazon – podcast

That answer to that question would be 45,000 sq km (17,400 sq miles) over Bolsonaro’s 2019-2022 period in office, roughly equivalent to the loss of more than a million trees a day, and 59.5% higher than the previous four years.

Dom never got to report on that. He too was cut down, murdered alongside Bruno on 5 May 2022 close to the Javari Valley indigenous territory while he was researching a book titled How to Save the Amazon.

The man who confessed to their killing was a fisher named Amarildo da Costa de Oliveira, who is now on trial. He apparently resented Bruno’s efforts to prevent him invading the indigenous territory, incursions that were illegal but encouraged by the president’s weakening of protections, rhetoric against environmental groups and tacit acceptance of lawlessness. As Dom had foreseen, Bolsonaro had made life more dangerous for journalists and the forest.

Jair Bolsonaro lost office later that year and was then convicted for attempting a military coup to overturn the election results. Dom had also anticipated this: “He is a criminal and I sincerely hope one day I see him being arrested by those federal police guys in the balaclavas in black,” he wrote in 2021.

I am sure Dom would have been cheered by last week’s government announcement of record low deforestation in the Amazon and the neighbouring Cerrado savanna thanks to strong enforcement during Lula’s current four-year term.

Such gains look precarious now that one of Bolsonaro’s “more extreme” sons is frontrunner in the presidential runoff and has promised, if he wins, to free his father and give him any job of his choice in the government.
Is there time for Lula to turn this around? How much worse could a second Bolsonaro family administration be? How much life – people, trees and other species – will die if they return to power?
I wish Dom were still around to discuss that.

articles.title: British woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling trip
articles.summary: Mother, 36, died after current off North Bimini reportedly swept away two boys, who were later rescued, police say
body: A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.
The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.
The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of North Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.
The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.
Bimini is a small island group between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.
The islands are best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and are also home to a world-leading shark research centre.

In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.

“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”
An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.
A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”

articles.title: ‘We can’t let the far right take power again’: Lula voters in final push before Brazil runoff
articles.summary: In bellwether Minais Gerais, with polls about even, president’s supporters are striving to win over those who abstained or voted for Flavio Bolsonaro
body: Naiara Boroni, Nikolas Domingues and Jodersson Diego live in the same city and do not know one another, but said they had done the same thing in recent days: persuaded at least one person who had not voted for the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round to choose him in this Sunday’s runoff.

In Boroni’s case, it was her grandmother who had not turned out; in Domingues’s, a cousin who had chosen a candidate who finished fourth. But Diego achieved what to many sounds almost impossible in such a polarised country: he said he had persuaded a woman who voted for the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro to switch sides.

“She’s a student of mine and didn’t vote for Lula because of her evangelical church. I didn’t argue; I tried to explain that he wasn’t everything they said he was, and she said she had changed her mind,” said Diego, 33, a dance teacher from Belo Horizonte, the capital of the state of Minas Gerais.

Winning over voters who abstained or cast null votes, and flipping as many others as possible, is at the heart of Lula’s strategy as he tries to do what no presidential candidate has ever managed in Brazil: overturn a first-round defeat like the one he suffered to Bolsonaro on 5 October.

Lula received 3.8 million fewer votes than in 2022, when he ran against the senator’s father, then president Jair Bolsonaro – who would go on to lose the runoff and try to stage a coup, which failed after the heads of two of the three armed forces refused to join him.

Serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest, he chose his eldest son to stand in his place. Flávio Bolsonaro has said that, if elected, he will pardon his father and receive the presidential sash from him.
The senator won 5 million more votes than his father and saw his party sweep elections for congress, state governments and state legislatures, which made him the clear favourite for many analysts.

In the three weeks of campaigning since then, however, polls have shown the gap steadily narrowing, and the two are now about even, with Bolsonaro still slightly ahead, but only by fractions of a percentage point.

“The scenario is one of a very tight tie, but with Lula’s campaign performing markedly better in the runoff,” said political scientist Manoel Leonardo Santos, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais.

The incumbent’s hopes rest on the narrowest-ever gap between first and second place, at less than 2% of the vote, while abstention reached a record 21%, which tends to hurt Lula more because it is more common among groups that favour him, such as lower-income and less-educated voters and older people.

Of the 10 cities with the highest abstention rates, eight are in Minas Gerais, the country’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo and a historical bellwether in presidential elections. No candidate has ever won nationally without carrying the state, where Lula now finished almost five percentage points behind Bolsonaro.

“If Lula’s voters turn out, he can win, but there is absolutely no guarantee that he will manage to make that happen,” said political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles, also a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais.
Bolsonaro supporters are also trying to keep mobilisation high.

Last Tuesday, at an event with local politicians that included an appearance by the senator via video call on a big screen, as well as a 23ft inflatable figure of his father, Minas Gerais governor-elect Cleitinho Azevedo urged the dozens of people present “not to think that we have already won the election and keep asking for votes”.

Pharmacist Magda Aparecida Araújo, 44, lives in the working-class neighbourhood next to the exhibition centre and was sitting in the back row. “I’m not going to belittle Lula’s governments, because I went to university thanks to a scholarship, but I now vote for Bolsonaro because he defends the family and I support traditional values,” said Araújo.

Given its electoral importance, both Lula and Bolsonaro chose the state capital for some of their final rallies: the senator’s was scheduled for this morning, while the incumbent held his last Wednesday.

“I’m here because we can’t let the far right take power again and destroy all of our rights,” said student Ester Nascimento, 17, who was with friends her own age, a symbol of what many see as perhaps the main catalyst behind Lula’s hopes of a comeback: young people who organically took to the streets in large protests all across Brazil.
“I think everyone felt obliged to make their voice heard,” said Nascimento.

Following advice from young, digitally native politicians, Lula’s team overhauled his online communications, and the 81-year-old incumbent, who does not even own a mobile phone, began recording selfie videos. Millions of his supporters joined a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where congressman André Janones sent dozens of daily instructions on how to make pro-Lula content go viral, and for the first time, the president’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s.

Lula also approved a “package of benefits” at the limits of what electoral law allows, including increasing and bringing forward payments from the main cash-transfer programme for poor families, while also securing a major political victory by getting congress to approve a shorter working week that could affect 30 million workers.
Even so, many analysts see much of the narrowing gap in the polls as driven more by Bolsonaro losing support, with his rejection rate having risen while Lula’s has fallen slightly.

Experts say some of Bolsonaro’s recent moves may have alienated the indecisive voters, including what was seen as an aggressive performance in the first presidential debate and a controversial speech in which he said he would use the new highly conservative congress to “change the constitution and re-democratise this country”.
That was the first warning sign that led administrative assistant Douglas Pereira Melo, 25, who voted for far-right influencer Renan Santos three weeks ago, to now choose Lula.

“It’s very dangerous for him to say that he’ll change the constitution. His father tried to stage a coup, and I’m afraid he’ll follow in his footsteps,” said Melo, adding that “the Bolsonaro scandals” had also weighed on his decision.

The senator is under investigation in two federal police inquiries, one into what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father, and another into alleged money laundering and a possible business partnership with a close friend, the betting-sector businessman and lawyer Willer Tomaz.

The senator is also embroiled in a dispute with the footballer Richarlison, who accuses Bolsonaro and Tomaz of conspiring to strip him of a mansion on an island, while Piauí magazine revealed last Thursday that, at the height of the Covid pandemic in 2020, the senator attended a barbecue on a boat with sex workers and lobbyists who were negotiating vaccine purchases with his father’s administration.
Political scientist Manoel Leonardo Santos said he has “no doubt” that Lula will enter the runoff with better chances than he did immediately after Bolsonaro’s first-round victory.
“Whether it will be enough for him to turn it around, we can’t say. But Lula has gained ground while Bolsonaro appears to have stopped growing,” he added.

articles.title: Opposition deepfake video of Spanish PM’s wife sparks outrage before election
articles.summary: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing
body: A political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister’s wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the deeply polarised country gears up for general elections next month.

Launched this week across the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks.

An AI-generated version of Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, for example, speaks about receiving a university post thanks to her husband’s job, while a deepfake of the former Socialist president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero speaks about hiding jewellery in a safe. Both lines are nods to ongoing investigations in which Gómez and Zapatero have denied any wrongdoing.

The Socialist party was swift to respond to the video, which by Friday had racked up nearly 2m views. “It’s telling people a colossal lie, and for a party to do it on its official accounts seems intolerable to me,” Óscar López, Spain’s digital transformation minister, told the broadcaster TVE on Friday.

While the video noted at the bottom – in tiny, nearly transparent font – that it had been created with AI, López pointed to the wider risk. “It’s very easy for anyone who isn’t used to AI to confuse that video with reality,” he said. “And call me crazy, but that seems extremely serious to me.”

On Friday, one of those whose likeness was used in the video filed a legal challenge against the PP, calling on the party to immediately take down the campaign advert. In a court complaint, Leire Díez, a former Socialist party member, reportedly accused the PP of defamation and digital identity theft, after the video used her likeness to hint at accusations that she worked to undermine judicial and law enforcement in order to help the Socialists.

A majority of the nine legal experts consulted by the newspaper El País concurred that what the PP had done was not illegal, given that the video was labelled as AI-generated and that the overall tone was one of political satire. “Given the context, everyone knows those people didn’t say those things,” Íñigo Navarro, a former dean of the faculty of law at Madrid’s Comillas Pontifical University, told the paper.

But the legality of the video was just one aspect, said Juan Antonio Lascuraín, a professor of criminal law at the Autonomous University of Madrid. “It’s quite another matter to ask whether it’s appropriate, exemplary or ethically and politically correct.”
Many sought to contextualise the videos within the wider effort – under way by officials across much of the world – to crack down on the impact of disinformation.

“It’s truly regrettable that the official account of a party that claims to want to govern and revitalise democracy is using AI-generated deepfakes in its campaign,” said José Javier Olivas, an associate professor who researches populism, conspiracy theories and AI biases at Spain’s National University for Distance Education.

He pointed to the wider backdrop of the election campaign, in which both mainstream parties have sought to rally voters by stoking emotions and attacking the morality of their rivals, but he said the video was a “red line” in terms of how campaigns normally unfolded.
“You’re using the images of other people, putting words in their mouths that they’re not saying, [and] this qualifies for disinformation,” he said.

The use of AI to generate or enhance political ads has also become a talking point in the US ahead of next month’s midterm elections. A recent report by a research group based at Wesleyan University in Connecticut identified more than 200 such ads, the vast majority of them tied to the Republicans.

“AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, a co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project. “For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle. Much of the AI use is not disclosed through any type of disclaimer.”

In Spain, the PP has brushed off criticism. “If there had been malicious intent to make people believe that the characters who appear there are real, then we’d have a problem,” Borja Sémper, of the party, told reporters. “But everyone can see that this is a way of using digital tools to highlight the hypocrisy in which the Socialist party operates.”
Most polls suggest the PP will win the 29 November general election but will need to rely on the support of the far-right Vox party to form a government.

articles.title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?
articles.summary: Established under the Franco dictatorship, the lunchtime ritual is in decline but all is not lost
body: A little before lunchtime each working day across Spain, evidence of one of the lingering, if less notorious, legacies of the Franco dictatorship is carefully traced in chalk, marker pen and printer ink.

Beckoning to hungry workers from blackboards, whiteboards and pieces of paper hastily taped to windows, the competitively priced menú del día, or daily set-price lunch, has been part of everyday Spanish life for more than half a century. But while 4m menús are still served each weekday, Spain is slowly losing its appetite for the familiar ritual.

Back in 2009, the country’s best-known chef, Ferran Adrià, went so far as to pronounce it dead – a victim of changing eating habits, economic downturns and bistro-style restaurants trying to charge €20-€30 (£17-£25) for what should be a simple starter, a hearty main and a choice of pudding or coffee … with bread and a drink thrown in.

Seventeen years later, however, the diagnosis seem a little premature. A new book by the Spanish food journalist Lakshmi Aguirre charts the history and evolution of the menú and argues that while the tradition is indeed in hot water, it hasn’t quite had its chips.

Her book – Menú del Día: Everyday Scenes of a First Course, a Second Course and Pudding – begins with the unpalatable fact that it all began with a tourist menu dreamed up in the mid-1960s up by the Spanish dictator Francisco Franco’s information and tourism minister, Manuel Fraga.

The regime was keen in the aftermath of the “years of hunger” that followed the Spanish civil war to show foreign visitors that food was plentiful, good and affordable. So it was that establishments serving food should offer “a starter of soup, a main course chosen from at least three options and based on egg, fish or meat and accompanied by a side dish, and a pudding based on fruit, something sweet, or cheese”.

The price was set at between 50 and 250 pesetas and, to stop unscrupulous restaurant owners watering down the drinks, the law stipulated that the accompanying quarter-litre of vino had to be “reds and whites from Spain that are pure, clean, pleasant on the palate and with an alcohol content of not less than 12%”.

In the early 1970s, the menú del día was rebaptised to make it look less like an attempt to woo – and sometimes gouge – tourists, but also to give ordinary Spaniards the idea that they, too, could indulge.

It is now so ubiquitous that many in Spain have no idea of its genesis. “When I was working on the book and people asked me about the menú del día, I’d mention Manuel Fraga and lots of them would throw their hands up in shock,” Aguirre said. “Some people know, but the vast majority don’t. It says a lot about us Spaniards; we forget very quickly.”
Researching the book, which includes personal reminiscences and a hefty selection of recipes, led Aguirre to consider the place of the menú in the popular consciousness.

“It’s part of our history, yet it’s changed over the years, reflecting the evolution of Spanish society,” she said. “It originated from something as terrible as a dictatorship, and today it has become a deeply ingrained custom. We feel a sense of nostalgia as we realise it’s fading away.”

The threats to the set lunch, whose average price today is €14.70, are many. Increasingly time-poor, many Spaniards now opt for a quick lunch, eating food from home at work or popping to a supermarket for a ready meal to microwave in a soulless canteen. Rising energy and food prices are making it harder for small, family-run restaurants to offer a rotating daily selection of starters and mains.

All of which explains the rise of the “dish of the day”, which offers restaurants a cheaper alternative to the traditional choice of three or four mains, and the increasing diversity of some menús, which now feature Latin American staples as a reflection of Spain’s changing demographics.

“The menú del día purists reject such options, but it has always been a reflection of the society that consumes it – and that’s exactly how it should be,” Aguirre said. “Spain today isn’t the same as it was in the 1980s, it is far more diverse and pluralistic, and as a result diners have changed as well. The menú del día exists for those who need it, for people who may come from many different backgrounds.”
Aguirre’s menú of choice would be a simple but well-cooked vegetable stew followed by hake in green sauce or baby squid in ink, and then leche frita (fried custard) or rice pudding.

But, as she points out in her book, the surroundings are almost as important as the cooking. Her benchmarks for a good menú del día spot include simple dishes, a regularly changing menu, chips that aren’t frozen, a chorus of regulars and “a chalkboard free of any trace of words such as avocado, burrata, tartare, truffle or sourdough bread”.
That chalkboard should, by preference, be written “by someone who’s never heard of lettering”, and bonus points are awarded if the child of the owners is doing their homework on a table down the end.
As it hobbles slowly towards what may be its demise, the menú del día has become something that transcends a filling and reasonably priced midday meal.

“What’s being lost is a meeting point,” Aguirre said. “A centre of community gravity where families with limited financial means can afford to eat out, and where those who live alone can find some company during a meal, which remains a deeply social activity.

“It’s a place where joys, sorrows and problems can be shared, or where you can simply enjoy a bit of breathing space, as well as a place for those who live far away or who don’t have the time to go home for lunch.”
The true privilege of the menú, she added, lay “not just in being able to pay for a meal, but also in having the time to enjoy it”.

articles.title: France to deploy 70,000 police on Saturday to prevent civil unrest
articles.summary: Security forces to include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism after worst street violence in years
body: France will deploy about 70,000 police around the country on Saturday as the government seeks to prevent more civil unrest after some of the worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost-of-living protests last weekend.

The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on ⁠Friday ⁠the security forces would include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism operations and hostage rescues, adding that there had been social media calls for violence from “ultra-left” groups.

“We are not talking about ⁠a peaceful, friendly demonstration,” Nuñez ​told reporters after a meeting of senior ministers and officials chaired by the president, Emmanuel Macron. “We ​are ​ready tomorrow ​to be ‌extremely firm ​and ​not tolerate anything.”

Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais – where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display – are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend program.

Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend’s hotspots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.

Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has caught it off guard six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday.
Related: Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases

Largely peaceful demonstrations were hijacked by groups of determined rioters, degenerating into rampant violence and extensive looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities. In Limoges, the town hall was set on fire and partly destroyed.

“We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all who commit violence,” Nuñez said, adding that besides 10,000 more police, the operation would include water cannon, armoured vehicles, mounted police, helicopters and drones.

Demonstrations are expected in several other countries this weekend, triggered by a broader, continent-wide wave of discontent over declining public services, housing affordability, public sector budget cuts and the spiralling cost of living.

Protests over related grievances have been called for Saturday in Milan, Rome and Turin in Italy; in Vienna, Austria; and in Madrid, Barcelona and other cities in Spain, as well as in Lisbon and Porto in Portugal, Dublin in Ireland and Tirana in Albania.

Protests are expected across France on Saturday, although several cities have banned demonstrations or forced them to change their planned routes to protect shops and public buildings, and forecast heavy rain and high winds could dampen turnout.

The centres of Lyon and some other large cities will be off-limits to protesters, while authorities in Paris authorised a union march along a limited route in the east of the capital between the Places de la Bastille and Nation that will avoid the city centre.

But requests for rallies in Paris organised by France’s main student union, UNEF, and the gilets jaunes movement, whose nationwide protests rocked France in 2018 and which plans 600 small-scale events around France on Saturday, were refused.

UNEF said its rallies, which grew from high school protests last month against teacher shortages and dilapidated facilities, would go ahead regardless. Several of the best-known cultural institutions in Paris, including the Louvre, said they would close on Saturday.

Authorities in Marseille had also banned all protests, but announced on Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis”. It will be the only authorised protest in the southern Bouches-du-Rhône department.
Related: ‘An orchestra being gassed should be an alarm signal’: the musical activists targeted in Paris

Unionists and opposition leaders have criticised the government for refusing to allow more rallies on Saturday, a decision being challenged in court in several cities. Marylise Léon of the CFDT union federation accused Macron of an abuse of authority.

“It’s ​counterproductive because there is a lot ​of anger and a demand to be considered and to be listened to,” Léon, the CFDT’s general secretary, told TF1 TV. “It’s not for the president to decide who can legitimately protest.”

La France Insoumise, the radical left party of Jean-Luc Mélenchon, said the government had “crossed the lines that separate a democracy from an authoritarian and police state”, adding that the bans would only “generate more chaos”.

Adding to the tensions, the far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner for next spring’s presidential elections, is due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orléans, drawing thousands of supporters – and leftwing, anti-racist opponents.

Nuñez was due to visit the city on Friday to “inspect the security arrangements” at the request of the prime minister’s office. The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 217 people – half of them first-time offenders – had been jailed since Saturday.

On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency”, saying gangs of rioters had been mainly responsible for the looting but the worst violence was caused by “ultra-left” groups seeking to “bring down the republic”.

Further stoking disquiet, one person was killed and four others injured – including a 12-year-old girl – in ⁠a shooting in the town of Trappes, west of Paris, on Friday in an attack that police said could have been racially motivated.

articles.title: Violence, intimidation and fear: 10 years on from the ‘Jungle’, life in Calais migrant camps is harsher than ever
articles.summary: People living in tents in northern France hoping to find asylum in England face increasing intimidation from police and far-right agitators
body: In the decade since the demolition of the “Jungle”, an area of Calais where thousands of asylum seekers set up makeshift shelters before embarking on Channel crossings to the UK, everything and nothing has changed.

This week, in a woodland clearing not far from one of Calais’s busy main roads, several brightly coloured tents are pitched. A jacket hanging from a tree branch blows in the brisk autumnal breeze alongside a belt decorated with union flags. It is only October but the wind makes the temperature feel several degrees chillier.

“I live in a tent,” says Adam*, at a nearby charity-run phone charging session. He is an electrical engineering student from Sudan who fled his country when the war started. “We have been evicted so many times. It is not worth having any possessions because the police take everything. I only have the clothes you can see me wearing now.”

Successive UK governments have spent hundreds of millions of pounds on numerous initiatives to curb illegal migration via northern France, including paying the French for police enforcement along the coast. On Wednesday Rob Jones, the director general of operations at the National Crime Agency, told MPs that thanks to UK-France efforts the business model of the people smugglers enabling small boat crossings was “starting to shake”.

Nonetheless more than 200,000 asylum seekers have made the journey from Calais to the UK since the “Jungle” – one of the largest of its kind in Europe – ceased to exist. On the 10th anniversary of it being torn down, about 4,000 people remain in smaller camps in Calais, Dunkirk and Boulogne, waiting to cross the sea.

The predominant nationalities hoping to reach the UK are almost the same as they were in 2016 – Eritreans, Sudanese, Somalis, Iranians and Afghans. Their resolve to reach the UK, where they believe they will be safe, has not weakened. Living conditions continue to be harsh and basic.

While the number of people arriving in the UK illegally on small boats has been steadily dropping, from more than 41,000 in 2025 to about 21,000 so far this year, this can in part be attributed to an overall reduction of irregular migration to Europe, as well as a large number of windy days – making Channel crossings more difficult.

In 2016 almost nobody crossed the Channel in small boats. But from 2018 onwards, small boat crossings began to rise. A policy of “zero point de fixation” was introduced in France to prevent the establishment of another large encampment. As a result, small living sites in wooded areas – particularly in Calais – are evicted on average once every 48 hours, with asylum seekers having tents, clothing and other possessions destroyed or confiscated by police in the process. Most will set up a new camp nearby, often with donations of tents from charities.
Human Rights Observers, an organisation set up to document the treatment of asylum seekers in northern France by authorities, described this cycle as the “border spectacle”.

Far-right agitators have travelled from the UK to harass people in the makeshift camps, leading French authorities to ban 10 people from entering the country. But more continue to arrive. Recently two agitators from Belgium and a third from Poland also travelled to northern France to harass and intimidate the asylum seekers.

Many at the phone charging session have attempted to cross the Channel to the UK several times. This week’s home affairs committee heard evidence that the average number of crossing attempts a person has increased from three to seven.

Treatment by police is a much-discussed topic among those charging their phones. The French charity Utopia 56, which supports displaced and homeless people, says it has documented a 40% increase in violence by police towards asylum seekers between April and August 2026 compared with the same period last year.
Related: Life for the displaced in Calais – in pictures

“I understand that the police are doing their work but why do they have to be so aggressive?” says one boy at the session, who does not wish to be named. “They stop me so often in Calais even when I am not trying to cross. Life in Calais is too difficult, everyone wants to leave as quickly as possible. I’m 16, I’m too young for this life but I don’t have a choice.”
Human Rights Observers counted 539 evictions of 3,792 people in Calais last year. They say firewood used for warmth and cooking is seized during evictions.
Project Play, which supports displaced children and families in northern France, also says they have observed an increase in aggressive behaviour by police.

“In recent years, we have seen an escalation in violence against everyone at the border – including children and families,” Katie Hall, advocacy lead at Project Play, said. “This year, we have also seen the police forcibly separating families, including by preventing parents from reaching children already on boats by taking hold of their other children.
“This is catastrophic for human rights, and reflects a politics devoid of empathy and humanity.”
With his phone fully charged, Adam leaves the session with a cheerful wave, carrying several takeaway containers of food provided by the charity to share with friends in neighbouring tents.

“I don’t know if I will ever find a way of continuing my degree but for now I am just trying to find somewhere I won’t be evicted from every two days,” he says. “I would like to reach the UK because I can speak English. But I am scared of the water so don’t want to get into a dinghy. I am trying to claim asylum in France. There is no straight road to safety.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian diesel tankers headed for North America, says Moscow, as US tries to revive peace talks
articles.summary: Tankers part of US-Russia deal that could see 500,000 metric tonnes of fuel supplied to world market this month. What we know on day 1,704
body: Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their ⁠way to North America, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak said ⁠on Friday. In ​a statement quoted by Russian news agencies, Novak said the cargoes were ⁠part of a deal that could see Russian companies supply 500,000 metric tonnes to US and world markets in October. “The first ⁠three fuel tankers are already on their ​way to the eastern ‌coast of ‌the Atlantic Ocean, with significant support from the ‌RDIF (Russian Direct Investment Fund),” Novak said. Under a deal announced this month by US president Donald Trump, Russia agreed ‌to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel ​prices in return for Trump temporarily lifting US sanctions on Russian fuel. Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged ⁠medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes, loaded with ultra-low sulphur diesel, is expected to arrive in ‌the US on 7 November.

The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians. Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations. Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.

The Oleshky ceasefire comes as the US is trying to organise new talks aimed at ending the war. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US have agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three ⁠countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Zelenskyy said he hoped a meeting of the countries’ leaders would follow.

The peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by Trump seen as favouring Russia, including limitations being placed on the Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem accessing the system, he would straighten it out ​and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

As the UK government prepares next week for the first budget under Andy Burnham’s leadership, EU leaders have pressed the new prime minister at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort. EU officials say Canada and Japan also should do more to support Ukraine.

The UN nuclear watchdog IAEA said ⁠Fiday ​that repairs to key ⁠power infrastructure near Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power ​plant ‌had been completed ‌under a ‌temporary ceasefire it brokered.
